questions.question: What is a thread in Java? Explain the `Thread` class vs `Runnable`, how threads map to OS threads, and when multithreading pays off.
questions.title: What Is a Thread in Java — `Thread`, `Runnable`, and Multithreading Explained
questions.direct_answer: A thread is an **independent path of execution within a JVM process**, sharing heap memory but having its own stack and program counter. Java threads are **1:1 mapped to OS native threads** on all mainstream JVMs (HotSpot, OpenJ9) — each platform thread costs ~0.5–1 MB of stack memory and is scheduled by the OS. You create them by **implementing `Runnable`** (preferred — preserves your single inheritance slot and works with `ExecutorService`) or extending `Thread` (legacy). **Multithreading pays off** for three workloads: CPU-bound parallelism (dividing work across cores), I/O concurrency (overlapping waits), and responsiveness (keeping UI/event loops free). As of Java 21, **virtual threads** (Project Loom) give you millions of cheap, JVM-scheduled threads ideal for I/O-bound servers.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate has a mental model of threads as independent execution paths sharing memory, understands `Thread` vs `Runnable`, and can articulate why concurrency matters
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking threads have separate memory — they share heap. Calling `thread.run()` instead of `thread.start()` and wondering why everything runs on the main thread
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention 1:1 OS thread mapping, the ~1 MB stack cost per platform thread, `ExecutorService` as the modern way to create them, and Java 21 virtual threads for I/O-bound workloads

sections.title: A Thread Is an Independent Execution Path Inside One JVM Process
sections.content:
A Java process contains one JVM, and that JVM can run many threads simultaneously. Each thread is an **independent sequence of instructions** with its own **stack** (local variables, call frames) and **program counter** — but all threads **share the heap** and loaded classes of the process.

This shared-heap model is what makes threads powerful and dangerous:
- Powerful — passing data between threads is free; you just share an object reference.
- Dangerous — two threads reading and writing the same field without coordination produce **race conditions** and memory visibility bugs that are notoriously hard to reproduce.

On all mainstream JVMs (HotSpot on Linux/Mac/Windows, OpenJ9), every Java `Thread` is **1:1 mapped to an OS native thread** — `pthread_create` on Linux/Mac, `CreateThread` on Windows. The OS scheduler decides which thread runs on which core and when to preempt it. Each platform thread costs roughly **512 KB–1 MB of stack memory** by default (tunable via `-Xss`), so practically you can run 1,000–10,000 of them before hitting memory or scheduling limits.

Java 21 changed this landscape with **virtual threads** — lightweight threads scheduled by the JVM on top of a small pool of platform threads. You can create millions of them.

sections.title: Three Ways to Create a Thread — And Which One to Actually Use
Why Bother with Threads — Three Workloads That Need Them
sections.content:
**CPU-bound parallelism** — dividing computation across cores. Matrix multiplication, image processing, batch analytics. On an 8-core machine, a well-parallelized CPU workload runs close to 8× faster. Libraries: `parallelStream()`, `ForkJoinPool`, Fork/Join framework, `CompletableFuture`.

**I/O concurrency** — overlapping slow operations. A web server serving 10,000 clients, each waiting on a database or remote API. While thread A waits for its HTTP response, thread B processes another request. Without threads, you'd serve one client at a time. This is where **virtual threads shine** in Java 21.

**Responsiveness** — keeping the UI, event loop, or main thread free. A Swing/JavaFX app spawns background threads so the UI thread stays responsive. A game engine runs physics, rendering, and audio on separate threads. Spring Boot web servers dedicate the main thread to accepting connections and delegate request handling to a pool.

**When threading does NOT help**:
- Tiny tasks (< microseconds) — thread creation and coordination overhead dominates.
- Problems that are inherently sequential (hash chaining, some algorithms).
- Already CPU-saturated workloads — adding threads just adds contention.

Amdahl's Law: speedup is capped by the serial portion of the work. If 10% of a task is inherently sequential, you're capped at 10× speedup no matter how many cores.

sections.title: Platform Threads vs Virtual Threads — The Java 21 Split
sections.content:
Before Java 21, every Java thread was a **platform thread** — one-to-one with an OS thread. That's ~1 MB of stack, OS scheduling, and a practical limit around 5,000–10,000 threads on a server.

Java 21 introduced **virtual threads** (Project Loom). They're **M:N scheduled**: the JVM multiplexes many virtual threads onto a small pool of carrier platform threads. When a virtual thread calls a blocking operation (I/O, `Thread.sleep`, lock acquisition on `ReentrantLock`), the JVM **unmounts** it from its carrier and parks it cheaply in a continuation. Another virtual thread can use that carrier.

**Platform threads** — use for:
- CPU-bound work (virtual threads give no benefit; they still need a carrier).
- Native code that expects a stable OS thread.
- Code that uses `synchronized` on long I/O (virtual threads get **pinned** and stop scaling).

**Virtual threads** — use for:
- I/O-bound servers handling many concurrent requests.
- Request-per-thread frameworks (Spring, Jakarta EE) that previously maxed out at ~10k concurrent requests.
- Simple blocking code that you used to rewrite reactively.

`Thread.ofVirtual().start(runnable)` or `Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()` create them. They look and behave like regular threads but are essentially free to create.

sections.title: The Anatomy of a Running Thread — What You Share and What's Private
sections.content:
Per-thread (isolated):
- **Stack** — call frames, local variables, method parameters.
- **Program counter** — current instruction.
- **`ThreadLocal` values** — one slot per thread in a shared `ThreadLocalMap` on the thread object.
- **Thread name, priority, daemon flag, `UncaughtExceptionHandler`**.

Shared across all threads in the JVM:
- **Heap** — all objects allocated by `new`.
- **Method area / Metaspace** — class metadata, static fields.
- **File descriptors, sockets, system resources** — opened via shared OS handles.

The shared heap is exactly what makes coordination necessary. When two threads write to the same field:
- Without synchronization, one can lose its update (race condition).
- Without `volatile` or locks, one might never see the other's write (memory visibility).
- Without atomicity, a read-modify-write sequence can produce nonsensical intermediate values.

Java's solution: the **Java Memory Model (JSR 133)**, `synchronized` blocks, `volatile` fields, `java.util.concurrent.atomic` classes, and concurrent collections. That's why threads require more care than they initially appear.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- A thread is an **independent execution path within a JVM process**, with its own stack but shared heap.
- On all mainstream JVMs, Java **platform threads are 1:1 mapped to OS threads**; each costs ~1 MB of stack.
- **`Runnable` over extending `Thread`** — decouples task from thread, enables lambdas and `ExecutorService`.
- Use **`ExecutorService`** instead of `new Thread(...)` in production.
- **`Callable<V>`** returns a value and can throw checked exceptions; pairs with `Future<V>`.
- Threads solve three workload types: **CPU parallelism**, **I/O concurrency**, **responsiveness**.
- **Java 21 virtual threads** are cheap, M:N scheduled, ideal for I/O-bound servers; avoid for CPU-bound work or code with `synchronized` on long I/O.
- Shared heap means **race conditions** and memory visibility are concerns — that's what `synchronized`, `volatile`, and concurrent collections address.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
A thread is an **independent execution path inside one JVM process**.

**What's isolated per thread**
- Stack (local variables, call frames)
- Program counter
- `ThreadLocal` values

**What's shared**
- The heap — all objects allocated with `new`
- Method area, loaded classes, static fields
- File descriptors and system resources

**This shared-heap model is the core of both power and danger**
- Power: passing data between threads is free — share an object reference
- Danger: uncoordinated reads and writes cause race conditions and visibility bugs

**On mainstream JVMs, platform threads are 1:1 with OS threads**
- `pthread_create` on Linux, `CreateThread` on Windows
- ~512 KB to 1 MB of stack per thread (tunable with `-Xss`)
- Practical limit: 5,000–10,000 platform threads per server
- The OS scheduler, not the JVM, decides when each runs

**Three ways to create threads**
- **Extend `Thread`** — legacy; wastes single inheritance slot
- **Implement `Runnable`** — preferred; functional interface so lambdas work; decouples task from thread
- **`ExecutorService`** — the modern default; submit `Runnable` or `Callable` tasks to a pool
- **`Callable<V>`** is `Runnable` plus return value and checked-exception support

**When multithreading actually helps**
- **CPU-bound parallelism** — dividing work across cores (up to Amdahl's limit)
- **I/O concurrency** — overlapping slow network or disk waits
- **Responsiveness** — keeping UI or event loops free while background work runs

**Java 21 virtual threads changed everything for I/O workloads**
- M:N scheduled — JVM multiplexes millions of virtual threads on a small platform-thread carrier pool
- When a virtual thread blocks on I/O, it unmounts from its carrier cheaply
- `Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()` is the idiom
- Use for I/O-bound servers; avoid for CPU-bound work or code with `synchronized` on long I/O (pinning problem)

**Recommendation:** In modern code, don't call `new Thread(...)` directly. Reach for `ExecutorService` for bounded pools on CPU work, or `Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()` on Java 21+ for I/O-bound request handling. Always prefer `Runnable` or `Callable` over extending `Thread`. Remember that the heap is shared — any mutable state accessed from multiple threads needs coordination via `synchronized`, `java.util.concurrent`, or immutability.

questions.title: Thread vs Runnable vs Callable
questions.question: What are the differences between extending Thread, implementing Runnable, and implementing Callable when creating threads in Java?

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands Java's concurrency primitives and can choose the right abstraction for the task.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing Callable with Runnable — Callable can return a value and throw checked exceptions; Runnable cannot.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that Thread itself implements Runnable, and discuss how Callable integrates with ExecutorService via Future/FutureTask.

questions.direct_answer: Runnable is the preferred low-level task abstraction (no return value, no checked exceptions). Callable is used when you need a return value or need to propagate checked exceptions. Extending Thread is discouraged because it tightly couples task logic to thread lifecycle.

sections.title: Extending Thread Wastes Your Single Inheritance Slot — But the Real Question Is Return Values and Exceptions
sections.content:
The interview question seems simple — Thread vs Runnable vs Callable — but the real depth is in understanding **why each exists** and when the distinction matters in modern Java.

**Extending Thread** is the pre-Java 5 approach. It works but wastes your single inheritance slot and couples the task logic to the threading mechanism. You cannot submit a Thread subclass to an ExecutorService.

**Implementing Runnable** separates the task from the thread. `Runnable.run()` returns void and cannot throw checked exceptions. This is the minimum interface — any task that produces no result and handles its own errors.

**Implementing Callable<V>** is the key upgrade. `Callable.call()` returns a value of type V and can throw checked exceptions. Submit a Callable to an ExecutorService and you get a `Future<V>` — a handle to retrieve the result, check completion, or cancel the task.

In modern Java (5+), you almost never create Thread objects directly. **ExecutorService** manages the thread pool, and you submit Runnables or Callables. The choice between Runnable and Callable depends solely on whether you need a return value or need to propagate checked exceptions.

sections.title: Return Values, Exceptions, and ExecutorService Compatibility
sections.content:
The table shows that the real decision is between Runnable and Callable — Thread extension is obsolete.

| Feature | extends Thread | Runnable | Callable<V> |
|---|---|---|---|
| Method | `run()` | `run()` | `call()` |
| Return type | void | void | V (generic) |
| Checked exceptions | Cannot throw | Cannot throw | Can throw |
| Submit to ExecutorService | No | Yes — `execute()` or `submit()` | Yes — `submit()` returns `Future<V>` |
| Single inheritance | Consumed | Preserved | Preserved |
| Lambda compatible | No | Yes (functional interface) | Yes (functional interface) |
| Cancel support | Manual via `interrupt()` | Via `Future.cancel()` | Via `Future.cancel()` |

Both **Runnable and Callable are functional interfaces** — you can express them as lambdas. `executor.submit(() -> computeResult())` is a Callable if it returns a value, or a Runnable if it does not. The compiler infers which based on the lambda body.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Extending Thread: legacy only** — wastes single inheritance slot; cannot be submitted to ExecutorService.
- **`Runnable`** — `run()` returns void, cannot throw checked exceptions; for fire-and-forget tasks.
- **`Callable<V>`** — `call()` returns a value, can throw checked exceptions; submit to get `Future<V>`.
- **Both are functional interfaces** — expressible as lambdas; compiler infers which based on whether the lambda returns a value.
- **`Future.get()` blocks; use `CompletableFuture`** — non-blocking composition, error handling, and chaining.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Java provides three ways to represent a concurrent task: extending `Thread`, implementing `Runnable`, or implementing `Callable`. In modern Java, extending Thread directly is considered legacy — tasks are expressed as Runnable or Callable and submitted to an ExecutorService, which manages threads as a pool.

**Three approaches:**
- Extending Thread: wastes your single inheritance slot; can't be submitted to ExecutorService — legacy only
- `Runnable`: `run()` returns void, cannot throw checked exceptions — for fire-and-forget tasks
- `Callable<V>`: `call()` returns a value, can throw checked exceptions — submit to get a `Future<V>`

**Both are functional interfaces:**
- Expressible as lambdas — compiler infers which based on whether the lambda returns a value
- `executor.execute(() -> doWork())` vs `Future<Result> f = executor.submit(() -> compute())`

**Beyond Future:**
- `Future.get()` blocks the calling thread — `CompletableFuture` is the modern upgrade with non-blocking composition, error handling, and chaining

I recommend Callable with CompletableFuture for most production scenarios. Never create `Thread` objects directly.

sections.title: RUNNABLE Does Not Mean Running — The Most Misunderstood Thread State
sections.content:
Most developers draw the thread lifecycle as NEW -> RUNNING -> TERMINATED and miss three critical states. The JVM defines **six states** in `Thread.State`, and the most misunderstood is RUNNABLE — which includes threads that are **waiting for CPU time**, not just threads actively executing on a core.

A thread starts in **NEW** (created but `start()` not called). Calling `start()` moves it to **RUNNABLE** — eligible for scheduling but not necessarily running. The OS scheduler decides when it actually gets CPU time. There is no separate RUNNING state in the Java enum.

**BLOCKED** means the thread is waiting to acquire a monitor lock — another thread holds the `synchronized` block it needs. **WAITING** means the thread called `Object.wait()`, `Thread.join()`, or `LockSupport.park()` without a timeout. **TIMED_WAITING** is the same but with a timeout — `Thread.sleep()`, `wait(millis)`, or `join(millis)`.

The distinction between BLOCKED and WAITING matters for diagnosis. A BLOCKED thread is stuck on a lock contention issue. A WAITING thread is deliberately parked, typically in a producer-consumer pattern. Thread dumps show both states, and knowing the difference tells you whether you have a locking problem or a design issue.

sections.title: State Transitions: What Triggers Each Change and How to Diagnose Stuck Threads
sections.content:
Understanding the transitions is essential for reading thread dumps in production.

**NEW to RUNNABLE**: `thread.start()`. Calling `start()` twice throws `IllegalThreadStateException` — the thread cannot be restarted.

**RUNNABLE to BLOCKED**: The thread tries to enter a `synchronized` block or method whose monitor is held by another thread. It stays BLOCKED until the lock is released.

**RUNNABLE to WAITING**: The thread calls `Object.wait()` (releases the monitor and waits for `notify()`), `Thread.join()` (waits for another thread to die), or `LockSupport.park()`. No timeout — it waits indefinitely.

**RUNNABLE to TIMED_WAITING**: Same triggers but with a timeout — `Thread.sleep(millis)`, `wait(millis)`, `join(millis)`, or `LockSupport.parkNanos()`. The thread returns to RUNNABLE when the timeout expires or the condition is signaled.

```java
Thread t = new Thread(() -> { /* task */ }); // NEW
t.start(); // RUNNABLE
synchronized (lock) { lock.wait(); } // WAITING
Thread.sleep(1000); // TIMED_WAITING
```

**Any state to TERMINATED**: The `run()` method completes (normally or via exception). Once TERMINATED, the thread cannot be restarted — create a new Thread instance instead.

In thread dumps, look for clusters of BLOCKED threads pointing to the same monitor — that indicates lock contention. WAITING threads on `Object.wait()` are typically in a correct producer-consumer pattern.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Six states in `Thread.State`** — NEW, RUNNABLE, BLOCKED, WAITING, TIMED_WAITING, TERMINATED.
- **RUNNABLE != currently executing** — the most common misconception; there is no separate RUNNING state in the Java enum.
- **BLOCKED = waiting for a synchronized monitor** — the lock-holder is identified in thread dumps.
- **WAITING = deliberately parked** — called `wait()`, `join()`, or `park()` without a timeout.
- **Cannot restart after TERMINATED** — calling `start()` again throws `IllegalThreadStateException`; use ExecutorService instead.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Java defines six thread states in `Thread.State` — and the most important thing to know is that RUNNABLE does not mean currently executing.

**States:**
- NEW: before `start()` is called
- RUNNABLE: eligible for CPU time — may or may not be actively running; there is no separate RUNNING state in the Java enum
- BLOCKED: waiting for a `synchronized` monitor held by another thread
- WAITING: called `wait()`, `join()`, or `park()` without a timeout — deliberately parked until signaled
- TIMED_WAITING: same but with a timeout — `sleep()`, `wait(millis)`
- TERMINATED: `run()` completed; cannot be restarted — calling `start()` again throws `IllegalThreadStateException`

**Debugging significance:**
- BLOCKED threads all pointing to the same monitor → lock contention; the lock-holder is shown in the dump
- Repeated identical RUNNABLE stacks → CPU-burning loop or spin
- WAITING threads → typically correct producer-consumer pattern

I recommend focusing on the BLOCKED vs WAITING distinction when reading thread dumps — it tells you whether you have a locking problem or a design-level wait.

familiarity_anchors: smallest unit of execution within a process
speakable_v2.hook: A Java thread has six lifecycle states, and the one that trips people up is what RUNNABLE actually means.

beats.text: A thread is the smallest unit of execution within a process. The JVM tracks where each one sits using the Thread.State enum. The six values are NEW, RUNNABLE, BLOCKED, WAITING, TIMED_WAITING, and TERMINATED.

Without these states, there's no way to reason about what a thread is actually doing. They give us a shared vocabulary with the JVM and the dump tools. A dump that shows BLOCKED tells us a thread is sitting on a monitor lock and waiting for it to release.

groups.heading: NEW
groups.text: Created but not yet started. The constructor ran, start() did not.

groups.heading: RUNNABLE
groups.text: Eligible for CPU. The thread might be running on a core right now, or sitting in the OS run-queue waiting its turn.

groups.heading: BLOCKED
groups.text: Waiting to enter a synchronized block whose monitor lock another thread holds.

groups.heading: WAITING
groups.text: Parked indefinitely after wait, join, or LockSupport.park, until another thread signals it.

groups.heading: TIMED_WAITING
groups.text: The same idea as WAITING but with a deadline. Think sleep, wait(millis), or parkNanos.

groups.heading: TERMINATED
groups.text: run() finished and the thread's lifecycle is over. Java throws IllegalThreadStateException if you try start() a second time.

beats.text: Whatever shape we use, extends Thread or implements Runnable, the lifecycle's the same. Take Thread t = new Thread(runnable). That t starts out in NEW. Call t.start() and it moves to RUNNABLE. If run() hits a synchronized lock another thread holds, jstack shows t as BLOCKED. Once run() returns, t enters TERMINATED.

items: Don't read RUNNABLE as 'on the CPU right now'. Java doesn't separate ready-to-run from actually running.
BLOCKED is specifically about a synchronized monitor. WAITING is voluntary parking. The thread dump distinguishes them.
TERMINATED is sticky in the lifecycle. Calling start() on a finished thread throws, and there's no way to restart it.

speakable_v2.cap: Six states, one trap — RUNNABLE doesn't mean running. Read it as 'eligible' and the rest of the lifecycle falls into place.

questions.question: What's the difference between `Thread.start()` and `Thread.run()` in Java? Why is calling `run()` directly a bug?
questions.title: `Thread.start()` vs `Thread.run()` — Why Calling `run()` Directly Is a Classic Bug
questions.direct_answer: **`start()`** is a native method that asks the OS to create a new thread and have **that** thread execute `run()`. **`run()`** is just a regular instance method — calling it directly runs the code on the **current thread**, with no concurrency at all. `start()` can only be called **once per Thread instance** — the second call throws `IllegalThreadStateException`. Under the hood, `start()` registers the thread with the JVM, allocates the OS thread stack, invokes `pthread_create`/`CreateThread`, and the new native thread's entry point eventually calls your `run()`. This is the #1 "why doesn't my threaded code work" bug for beginners — `new Thread(task).run()` silently runs on the caller's thread instead of spawning.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate knows that `run()` is a normal method and `start()` is what actually creates a thread; the classic beginner bug that silently runs everything serially
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying `start()` just 'calls run()' — it does much more: allocates stack, registers with JVM thread group, invokes OS primitives. Also forgetting `start()` can only be called once
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Walk through what `start()` does internally (native `start0()`, OS thread creation, JVM bookkeeping), and note that `IllegalThreadStateException` on restart is because thread state machines don't allow TERMINATED → NEW

sections.title: The Difference Is Whether a New Thread Actually Exists
sections.content:
`run()` and `start()` look similar but do completely different things. This is the most common beginner bug in Java concurrency — and it manifests silently, with no exception, no warning, no log.

**`run()`** is declared in `Runnable` (and inherited by `Thread`). It's a **plain instance method** containing your task logic. Calling `thread.run()` is no different from calling `obj.doSomething()` — it executes synchronously on the **current thread**.

**`start()`** is declared in `Thread` as `public synchronized void start()`. It asks the JVM to create a new OS thread, register it, and arrange for **that new thread** to call `run()`. The call to `start()` itself returns immediately — you now have two threads running in parallel.

The classic bug:
```java
Thread worker = new Thread(() -> heavyComputation());
worker.run();    // BUG: runs on current thread, no parallelism
worker.start();  // CORRECT: spawns a new thread
```
If you accidentally call `run()`, your 'multi-threaded' code executes purely sequentially. No error, no hint — just unexpectedly slow performance and no actual concurrency. This is the #1 reason junior developers think 'threading doesn't work.'

sections.title: `start()` vs `run()` Side-by-Side
sections.content:
| Aspect | `start()` | `run()` |
|---|---|---|
| **Origin** | Declared in `Thread` | Declared in `Runnable`; overridden in `Thread` |
| **Effect** | Creates a new OS thread that then calls `run()` | Executes `run()` on the **current** thread |
| **Concurrency** | Yes — new thread runs in parallel | No — synchronous method call |
| **Thread state** | Transitions NEW → RUNNABLE | No state transition (thread stays in NEW) |
| **Can be called multiple times** | No — throws `IllegalThreadStateException` | Yes — it's a normal method |
| **Native code?** | Yes — delegates to native `start0()` | No — pure Java |
| **Returns** | Immediately (after spawning) | Only when `run()` finishes |
| **Thrown if misused** | `IllegalThreadStateException` if called twice | No exception — silent 'bug' |

sections.title: What `start()` Actually Does Under the Hood
sections.content:
`Thread.start()` is one of the most heavyweight calls in Java. Stepping through HotSpot's implementation (simplified):

1. **State check** — reads the thread's state. If not `NEW`, throws `IllegalThreadStateException`. That's why you can't restart a thread.
2. **Register with thread group** — adds `this` to the parent `ThreadGroup` for bookkeeping (legacy API, still used internally).
3. **Calls native `start0()`** — implemented in `Thread.c` / `os_linux.cpp`. This is where JVM meets OS.
4. **Inside the JVM**: allocates a `JavaThread` (C++ object representing the thread), creates its stack (default 1 MB), and sets up thread-local storage for JVM bookkeeping.
5. **Calls the OS primitive** — `pthread_create` on Linux/macOS, `CreateThread` on Windows. The OS allocates kernel resources, enqueues the thread, and returns.
6. **New thread bootstraps** — in `JavaThread::thread_main_inner`, it eventually invokes your Java `run()` through reflection.
7. **Back in the caller**, `start()` returns. The original thread continues; the new thread is now competing for CPU time on its own.

**Why `start()` is `synchronized`**: to guard the state check from concurrent calls from two different threads. Only one thread can successfully transition NEW → RUNNABLE.

**Cost**: creating a platform thread takes tens of microseconds and ~1 MB of memory. This is why pools and virtual threads exist.

sections.title: The Three Classic Bugs
Key Points
sections.content:
- **`run()` is a normal method** — calling it runs on the current thread, with zero concurrency.
- **`start()` creates a new OS thread** and arranges for it to call `run()`.
- **`start()` can be called exactly once per Thread instance** — second call throws `IllegalThreadStateException`.
- `start()` does heavy work: JVM bookkeeping, stack allocation, native `pthread_create`/`CreateThread`, thread group registration.
- Calling `run()` directly is a **silent bug** — no exception, just sequential execution and confusion.
- **Once a thread is TERMINATED, it cannot be restarted** — create a new Thread or use `ExecutorService`.
- Modern code should use **`ExecutorService`** or **virtual threads** instead of manually calling `start()`.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
`start()` and `run()` look similar but are completely different operations.

**`run()`** — a plain instance method
- Inherited from `Runnable`, overridden in `Thread`
- Calling `thread.run()` is just a method call; it executes on the **current thread**
- No concurrency, no new thread created

**`start()`** — a native method that creates a new OS thread
- Asks the JVM to allocate a thread stack, register bookkeeping, and call `pthread_create` (Linux/Mac) or `CreateThread` (Windows)
- That new OS thread then invokes your `run()`
- The original thread continues immediately — you now have two threads running in parallel
- Can only be called **once** per Thread instance; second call throws `IllegalThreadStateException`

**The classic beginner bug**
- `new Thread(task).run()` — no error, no warning, runs sequentially on the caller
- Developer thinks "threading doesn't work"
- `new Thread(task).start()` — the correct version; actually spawns

**What `start()` does under the hood**
- Checks that the thread is in `NEW` state (that's why it's `synchronized`)
- Registers with the parent `ThreadGroup`
- Calls native `start0()` which invokes the OS thread creation primitive
- Allocates ~1 MB of stack, sets up thread-local JVM storage
- Returns immediately while the new thread begins executing `run()`
- Cost: tens of microseconds plus the memory — this is why pools exist

**Why you can't restart a terminated thread**
- Once `run()` returns, the thread transitions to `TERMINATED`
- The state machine doesn't allow `TERMINATED` → `NEW`
- `start()` reads the state; throws `IllegalThreadStateException` if not `NEW`
- Need to execute the task again? Create a **new** Thread instance, or use `ExecutorService` which reuses underlying threads across many tasks

**Recommendation:** Don't call `start()` or `new Thread(...)` directly in production code. Submit tasks to `ExecutorService` (or `Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()` on Java 21+) and let the framework manage thread lifecycle. When you do see raw `Thread` in a code review, check immediately that the caller uses `start()`, not `run()` — it's a silent bug that often ships to production because tests pass (sequentially) and the performance issue only shows up under load.

questions.direct_answer: Daemon threads are background threads that do not prevent JVM shutdown. The garbage collector is the most well-known daemon thread.

sections.title: Daemon Threads Die When the Last User Thread Exits — and That Abrupt Shutdown Has Consequences
sections.content:
The JVM has a simple shutdown rule: it terminates when **all non-daemon (user) threads** have finished. Daemon threads are automatically killed — no `finally` blocks, no shutdown hooks for them, no graceful cleanup.

This makes daemon threads appropriate for **background housekeeping**: garbage collection, JMX monitoring, idle connection eviction. These tasks should run as long as the application runs and stop when it stops — no cleanup needed.

The mistake is using daemon threads for work that **must complete** — writing to a database, flushing a file, sending a network message. If the last user thread exits while a daemon thread is mid-write, the write is truncated with no exception, no log entry, no indication of failure.

A thread inherits its daemon status from the thread that created it. Threads created by the `main` thread are user threads by default. `setDaemon(true)` must be called **before** `start()` — calling it after throws `IllegalThreadStateException`.

ExecutorService thread pools created by `Executors.newFixedThreadPool()` use user threads by default. To create daemon thread pools, provide a custom `ThreadFactory` that sets `setDaemon(true)`. Spring's `@Async` uses daemon threads by default in some configurations — a surprising source of lost work if the application context shuts down before tasks complete.

sections.title: When Daemon Threads Are Safe and When They Lose Your Data
Key Points
sections.content:
- **JVM exits when all non-daemon threads finish** — daemon threads are killed immediately without `finally` block execution.
- **Appropriate for background housekeeping only** — cache eviction, heartbeats, metrics; tasks where incomplete execution is harmless.
- **`setDaemon(true)` before `start()`** — after throws `IllegalThreadStateException`; threads inherit daemon status from creator.
- **Danger: killed mid-write** — a daemon thread killed mid-database-write leaves the transaction inconsistent with no error.
- **For must-complete tasks** — use user threads with `ExecutorService.shutdown()` and `awaitTermination()`.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
The JVM exits when all non-daemon threads finish — daemon threads are killed immediately without running `finally` blocks or cleanup.

**Appropriate uses:**
- Background housekeeping: cache eviction, heartbeat pings, metrics collection
- Tasks where incomplete execution is harmless to data integrity

**Danger:**
- A daemon thread killed mid-database-write leaves the transaction inconsistent — no exception, no log, no indication of failure
- `setDaemon(true)` must be called before `start()` — after throws `IllegalThreadStateException`
- Threads inherit daemon status from their creator

**For tasks that must complete:**
- User threads with `ExecutorService.shutdown()` and `awaitTermination()` for graceful draining
- `Runtime.addShutdownHook()` for JVM shutdown coordination

I recommend daemon threads only for pure monitoring and housekeeping. For anything involving data persistence or state, use user threads with explicit shutdown coordination.

questions.question: What's the difference between `Thread.sleep()` and `Object.wait()` in Java? Which one releases the monitor lock?
questions.title: `Thread.sleep()` vs `Object.wait()` — Lock Release, Recipients, and When to Use Each
questions.direct_answer: Both pause a thread, but they behave fundamentally differently around locks. **`Thread.sleep(ms)`** is a **static method on `Thread`** that pauses the current thread for the given duration and **does NOT release any held monitor locks** — you still own every `synchronized` block you entered. **`Object.wait()`** is an **instance method on every `Object`**, must be called **while holding that object's monitor** (inside `synchronized(obj)`), **releases that monitor atomically as it parks the thread**, and requires `notify()`/`notifyAll()` (or a timeout) to wake up. In modern code, prefer **`LockSupport.park()`**, `ReentrantLock.Condition.await()`, or `BlockingQueue` — they're safer and more flexible. The interview depth is about the monitor-release semantics that make `wait/notify` the backbone of producer-consumer patterns.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate knows the lock-release semantics (the key difference), understands that `wait()` must be called inside a `synchronized` block, and can articulate the correct pairing with `notify`/`notifyAll`
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying `sleep()` releases the lock (it doesn't). Calling `wait()` without holding the monitor (throws `IllegalMonitorStateException`). Using `if` instead of `while` around `wait()` (fails to handle spurious wakeups)
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention spurious wakeups (why `wait()` must always be in a `while` loop), that `Thread.sleep(0)` is a yield hint, and that modern code should use `Condition.await()` or `LockSupport.park()` instead

sections.title: Both Pause — But Only One Releases the Lock
sections.content:
`Thread.sleep()` and `Object.wait()` both suspend the current thread, but they live at different layers of the concurrency stack.

**`Thread.sleep(long ms)`** — a **static method on `Thread`**. It tells the OS scheduler "park me for at least this long." The thread enters `TIMED_WAITING` state. When the time elapses (or the thread is interrupted), it re-enters `RUNNABLE`. **It does not interact with monitor locks at all** — if you called `sleep()` inside a `synchronized` block, you still own that lock, and no other thread can enter the block.

**`Object.wait()`** — an **instance method on every `Object`** (inherited from `Object`). You must be holding `obj`'s monitor to call `obj.wait()`; otherwise you get `IllegalMonitorStateException`. The call **atomically releases the monitor and parks the thread**. Another thread must acquire the same monitor and call `obj.notify()` or `obj.notifyAll()` to wake it up. When the waiter resumes, it **reacquires the monitor** before returning from `wait()`.

This lock-release is the whole point of `wait()`. It's what makes producer-consumer, condition variables, and every blocking queue possible. Without it, you'd deadlock — no one else could enter the `synchronized` region to signal you.

sections.title: `Thread.sleep()` vs `Object.wait()`
sections.content:
| Aspect | `Thread.sleep(ms)` | `Object.wait()` |
|---|---|---|
| **Type** | Static method on `Thread` | Instance method on `Object` |
| **Must hold monitor?** | No | Yes — `IllegalMonitorStateException` if not |
| **Must be in `synchronized`?** | No | Yes — inside `synchronized(this-same-object)` |
| **Releases monitor?** | **No** (keeps all held locks) | **Yes** (atomically) |
| **Thread state** | `TIMED_WAITING` | `WAITING` or `TIMED_WAITING` |
| **How it wakes up** | Timeout elapses or interrupt | `notify()`/`notifyAll()`, timeout, interrupt, or spurious wakeup |
| **Throws** | `InterruptedException` | `InterruptedException`, `IllegalMonitorStateException` |
| **Typical use** | Simple pause, polling, retry backoff | Condition signaling, producer/consumer |
| **Spurious wakeups?** | No | Yes — **must be in a `while` loop** |

sections.title: `wait()` Must Always Be in a `while` Loop — The Spurious Wakeup Rule
Producer-Consumer with `wait`/`notify` — Why the Lock Release Matters
The Modern Alternative — `Condition` and `BlockingQueue`
When to Use Each
sections.content:
**Use `Thread.sleep()`** for:
- Simple polling backoff (retry after delay).
- Demos, tests, simulated delays.
- Rate limiting in a single thread (though `ScheduledExecutorService` is usually better).

**Use `Object.wait()`** for:
- Condition signaling inside a `synchronized` block.
- Producer-consumer queues (but prefer `BlockingQueue`).
- Custom synchronizers on legacy code.

**Prefer modern alternatives** when:
- You need multiple wait conditions on the same lock → `ReentrantLock` + `Condition`.
- You need try-with-timeout or interruptibility → `Lock.tryLock`, `Condition.awaitNanos`.
- You're waiting for async results → `CompletableFuture`.
- You need a bounded/unbounded queue → `LinkedBlockingQueue`, `ArrayBlockingQueue`.

**Pitfalls for both**:
- `InterruptedException` must be handled — either rethrow, or re-set the interrupt flag with `Thread.currentThread().interrupt()` before continuing.
- `sleep()` held inside a `synchronized` block holds the lock for the entire sleep — watch for accidental contention.
- `wait()` outside `synchronized` throws `IllegalMonitorStateException`.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`sleep()` is static on `Thread`**; **`wait()` is instance on `Object`**.
- **`sleep()` keeps all held locks**; **`wait()` atomically releases the monitor of the object it's called on**.
- **`wait()` must be called inside `synchronized` on the same object** — else `IllegalMonitorStateException`.
- **`wait()` must be in a `while` loop** to handle spurious wakeups.
- Producer-consumer patterns rely on `wait()`'s lock release; `sleep()` cannot replace it.
- **Prefer `BlockingQueue`, `Condition`, or `LockSupport`** in modern code.
- Both throw `InterruptedException` — handle or propagate; don't swallow silently.
- `Thread.sleep(0)` is a yield hint, not truly zero pause.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Both pause a thread, but they behave completely differently around locks.

**`Thread.sleep(ms)`** — a **static method on `Thread`**
- Pauses the current thread for at least the given duration
- **Does not release any held locks** — if you're in a `synchronized` block, you still own it
- Thread state: `TIMED_WAITING`
- Wakes on timeout or interrupt
- Throws `InterruptedException`

**`Object.wait()`** — an **instance method on every `Object`**
- Must be called while holding that object's monitor — i.e., inside `synchronized(obj)`
- Otherwise throws `IllegalMonitorStateException`
- **Atomically releases the monitor and parks the thread**
- Another thread must reacquire the monitor and call `obj.notify()` or `notifyAll()` to wake it
- When it resumes, **reacquires the monitor before returning**

**Why the lock release matters**
- Producer-consumer: a full queue's producer calls `wait()`, releasing the lock so a consumer can enter `take()`, remove an item, and `notifyAll()`
- If `wait()` kept the lock, the system would deadlock immediately
- `sleep()` can't be used as a substitute here for exactly that reason

**The spurious wakeup rule**
- JVM spec explicitly allows `wait()` to return even without `notify()` or timeout
- Reason: OS condition variables like `pthread_cond_wait` allow it, and hiding it would be costly
- Therefore: **`wait()` must always be in a `while` loop** that re-checks the predicate
- Using `if` is a classic bug — a spurious wakeup proceeds with invalid state

**In modern code I rarely write raw `wait`/`notify`**
- `ReentrantLock` + `Condition.await()` — same semantics, multiple condition variables, try-lock
- `BlockingQueue` (`LinkedBlockingQueue`, `ArrayBlockingQueue`) — hides the whole pattern
- `LockSupport.park()` — low-level primitive underlying `j.u.c`
- `CompletableFuture` — for async composition

**Other gotchas**
- Both throw `InterruptedException` — handle it by rethrowing or resetting the interrupt flag; don't swallow silently
- `sleep()` inside `synchronized` holds the lock for the entire sleep — watch for contention
- `Thread.sleep(0)` is a yield hint, not truly zero

**Recommendation:** Never use `sleep()` for coordination — it's a delay, not a signal. Use `wait()`/`notify()` only if you're maintaining legacy code or building a custom synchronizer. For any new concurrent code, reach for **`BlockingQueue`** for producer-consumer, **`ReentrantLock` + `Condition`** for multi-condition signaling, or **`CompletableFuture`** for async flows. The monitor-release semantics of `wait()` are what make `synchronized` useful for coordination — once you understand that, the rest of Java's concurrency primitives make sense.

questions.question: How does thread interruption work in Java? Explain `interrupt()`, `isInterrupted()`, and `interrupted()`, and the correct way to respond to interrupts.
questions.title: Thread Interruption in Java — `interrupt()`, `isInterrupted()`, `interrupted()` Explained
questions.direct_answer: Java interruption is a **cooperative signal**, not a forced kill. `thread.interrupt()` sets the target thread's **interrupt flag** — a single boolean. The target thread must **voluntarily check** the flag (via `Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted()`) or be in a blocking call that's interrupt-aware (`sleep`, `wait`, `join`, `Lock.lockInterruptibly`, `BlockingQueue.take`). Blocking methods throw **`InterruptedException`** and **clear the flag**. `Thread.interrupted()` is a **static** method that reads and clears the flag for the current thread; `thread.isInterrupted()` is an **instance** method that just reads it. The golden rule: **never swallow `InterruptedException`** — either rethrow it, or re-set the flag with `Thread.currentThread().interrupt()` before continuing. `Thread.stop()` is deprecated and unsafe — interruption is the only supported way to request cancellation.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands that interruption is cooperative, knows the difference between `isInterrupted()` and `interrupted()`, and knows how to handle `InterruptedException` correctly (don't swallow!)
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Catching `InterruptedException` and doing nothing — the most common bug in Java concurrency code. Also confusing `interrupted()` (static, clears flag) with `isInterrupted()` (instance, preserves flag)
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that `InterruptedException` means 'flag was set AND I cleared it as part of throwing'; the restore pattern `Thread.currentThread().interrupt()`; `Future.cancel(true)` as the idiomatic way to interrupt a task; and non-interruptible blocks (`InputStream.read()` classic case)

sections.title: Interruption Is a Polite Request, Not a Kill Switch
sections.content:
Java once had `Thread.stop()`, which really did forcibly kill a thread mid-execution. It was so dangerous — corrupting locks, leaving data structures half-updated — that it was deprecated in 1998 and in 2026 it effectively doesn't work. The replacement is **interruption**: a cooperative signal that asks "please stop as soon as it's safe."

Every Thread has an **interrupt flag** — a single boolean bit. `thread.interrupt()` sets it. That's the entire mechanism. The thread doesn't stop. It doesn't throw an exception. It doesn't change state. Something **has to check** that flag for it to matter.

Who checks it?
- **Your code** — via `Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted()` inside long loops.
- **JDK blocking methods** — `sleep`, `wait`, `join`, `Lock.lockInterruptibly`, `BlockingQueue.take`, `Selector.select` — check the flag and throw `InterruptedException` to break out.
- **Channel I/O** — `InterruptibleChannel` methods throw `ClosedByInterruptException`.

Things that are **not** interruptible by default:
- Classic `InputStream.read()` on a socket — blocks forever regardless of interrupt. The workaround: close the socket, which causes `read()` to throw.
- `synchronized` block acquisition — uninterruptible. Use `ReentrantLock.lockInterruptibly()` instead.
- CPU-bound loops without an explicit check.

This is why well-written concurrent code peppers `isInterrupted()` checks at loop boundaries — otherwise, cancellation silently fails.

sections.title: The Three Methods — What Each Does and When to Use It
Handling `InterruptedException` — The Three Valid Responses
The Wrong Way — Interrupt Swallowed, Shutdown Broken
The Right Way — Restore the Flag and Exit Cleanly
Non-Interruptible Operations and the Workarounds
Key Points
sections.content:
- Interruption is **cooperative** — `interrupt()` sets a boolean flag; the target thread must check it.
- **`thread.isInterrupted()`** is instance, **preserves** the flag.
- **`Thread.interrupted()`** is static, reads the current thread's flag and **clears** it.
- Blocking methods (`sleep`, `wait`, `join`, `BlockingQueue.take`, `Lock.lockInterruptibly`) throw **`InterruptedException`** and **clear the flag**.
- **Never swallow `InterruptedException`** — either rethrow or restore with `Thread.currentThread().interrupt()`.
- **`synchronized` blocks and classic `InputStream.read()` are NOT interruptible** — use `ReentrantLock.lockInterruptibly` and close sockets respectively.
- `Future.cancel(true)` is the idiomatic way to interrupt a task.
- `Thread.stop()` is permanently deprecated and unsafe.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Java interruption is a **cooperative signal**, not a forced kill.

**The mechanism**
- Each thread has a boolean **interrupt flag**
- `thread.interrupt()` sets it — that's all
- The target thread must **voluntarily check** the flag, or be in a blocking call that checks for it

**Who checks the flag**
- JDK blocking methods: `sleep`, `wait`, `join`, `BlockingQueue.take`, `Lock.lockInterruptibly`, `Selector.select`
- They throw `InterruptedException` and **clear the flag** as part of the throw
- Your own loops should check with `Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted()`
- Interruptible channels (`FileChannel`, `SocketChannel` via NIO) throw `ClosedByInterruptException`

**Not interruptible**
- Classic `InputStream.read()` on a socket — must close the socket instead
- `synchronized` block acquisition — use `ReentrantLock.lockInterruptibly()`
- CPU-bound loops with no check — add periodic checks yourself

**The three methods**
- **`thread.interrupt()`** — sets the flag on another thread
- **`thread.isInterrupted()`** — instance method, **reads** the flag, doesn't clear it; safe for diagnostics
- **`Thread.interrupted()`** — static method, reads the current thread's flag and **clears** it; use when intentionally consuming

**The golden rule — never swallow `InterruptedException`**
- When a blocking method throws it, the flag is already cleared
- If you do nothing in the catch, the cancellation signal is permanently lost
- This is the #1 cause of "my Spring Boot app hangs on shutdown" tickets

**The three acceptable responses**
- **Propagate** — add `throws InterruptedException` and let the caller handle
- **Restore and exit** — call `Thread.currentThread().interrupt()` to re-set the flag, then return or break out of the loop
- **Wrap and throw** unchecked — e.g., `CancellationException` — after restoring the flag

**Using interruption in `ExecutorService`**
- `pool.shutdownNow()` interrupts all workers
- `future.cancel(true)` interrupts the running task; `false` just marks the future cancelled
- Workers should loop with `while (!Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted())` and restore the flag in catch blocks to exit cleanly

**The deprecated alternative**
- `Thread.stop()` forcibly killed threads mid-execution, corrupting locks and data
- Deprecated in 1998, permanently removed in recent JDKs
- Interruption is the only safe way to request cancellation

**Recommendation:** Treat `InterruptedException` as a first-class signal, never an inconvenience to silence. The standard pattern in every blocking catch block is `Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); return;` — that single line fixes the vast majority of shutdown-hang bugs. In loops, always gate the iteration on `!Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted()` and use `ReentrantLock.lockInterruptibly()` whenever a lock acquisition might take long. SonarQube rule S2142 catches swallowed `InterruptedException` — turn it on and enforce it in CI.
